questions.question: How does @InjectMocks injection work under the hood?
questions.title: @InjectMocks Injection Strategy | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: @InjectMocks tries three injection strategies in order: constructor injection (matching by type), setter injection, then field injection. If none succeed, it creates the object with no injection — no error is thrown, leading to null fields that cause NPE at runtime.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the internal resolution order of @InjectMocks and its silent failure mode
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming @InjectMocks will throw a clear error if injection fails — it does not, it silently continues with null fields
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the three-phase injection order and connect this to why constructor injection in production code prevents these silent failures

sections.title: How @InjectMocks Resolves Dependencies
sections.content:
When you annotate a field with **@InjectMocks**, Mockito tries to wire the mocks into your test subject using a three-phase strategy. First, it looks for a **constructor** that matches the available @Mock fields by type — it picks the largest constructor it can satisfy.

If no constructor match is found, it tries **setter methods** named like setDependencyName(). As a last resort, it uses **field injection** via reflection to directly assign mocks to matching fields. The silent danger: if all three phases fail, Mockito still creates the object but leaves unmatched fields as **null**. You won't see any error until a NullPointerException occurs during test execution. This is why explicit constructor injection in production code is safer — it forces compile-time checks and makes dependencies obvious.

sections.content:
amber|InjectMocks|~Builds the subject|gathers the Mock fields|injects them in|no manual wiring
blue|Injection Order|~Tries in sequence|constructor first|then setter|then field
emerald|Matching|~By type then name|ambiguous uses name|silent if it fails|nulls slip through

sections.title: Illustrating @InjectMocks Three-Phase Resolution
When to Rely on @InjectMocks
sections.content:
Use **@InjectMocks** when your class has simple, single-constructor dependency injection with all dependencies as @Mock fields. It reduces boilerplate for straightforward service tests.

Avoid it when you have **multiple constructors** or **conditional initialization logic** — Mockito's silent failure will hide configuration errors. In complex scenarios (like needing different mock configurations per test), prefer **manual construction** in @BeforeEach where you explicitly call the constructor with mocks. This makes the wiring visible and fails at compile time if you pass wrong types.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting an Error on Injection Failure**: Freshers assume @InjectMocks will throw an exception if a dependency can't be wired — it doesn't. It leaves the field null, causing cryptic NPE later.
- **Mixing Field and Constructor Injection**: Using @Autowired field injection in production code then wondering why @InjectMocks behaves unpredictably — the injection order becomes ambiguous.
- **Not Using @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)**: Forgetting this annotation means @Mock and @InjectMocks aren't processed, leaving everything null and causing test failures that look like mock issues but are actually initialization problems.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Three-Phase Order**: Constructor injection first (largest matching constructor), then setter injection, then field injection as fallback
- **Silent Failure**: If no injection strategy succeeds, Mockito creates the object with null fields — no exception is thrown
- **Constructor Preference**: Using constructor injection in production code aligns with Mockito's first phase and makes tests predictable
- **@ExtendWith Required**: Without MockitoExtension, @InjectMocks does nothing and all fields remain null
- **Manual Construction Alternative**: For complex scenarios, create the test subject manually in @BeforeEach with explicit constructor calls
- **Type Matching**: Mockito matches by type only, not by field name — having two mocks of the same type causes ambiguity
- **Final Fields**: @InjectMocks can only inject final fields via constructor injection — setter and field injection cannot modify final fields

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When you use at-InjectMocks, Mockito follows a three-step process to wire your mocks into the test subject. First, it tries constructor injection — it looks for the largest constructor that it can satisfy with the available at-Mock fields, matching by type. If that doesn't work, it tries setter injection, looking for methods like setDependencyName. If that also fails, it falls back to field injection using reflection to directly assign mocks to matching fields. Here's the tricky part: if all three phases fail, Mockito doesn't throw an error. It just creates the object and leaves unmatched fields as null. You won't discover the problem until your test runs and throws a NullPointerException. That's why constructor injection in production code is so important — it forces compile-time validation of dependencies and aligns perfectly with Mockito's first injection phase. In my tests, I use at-ExtendWith with MockitoExtension to make sure the annotations are processed. For complex setups where I need different mock configurations per test, I skip at-InjectMocks entirely and manually construct the service in at-BeforeEach, passing mocks explicitly. That way, the wiring is visible and any mismatch fails immediately at compile time.

questions.question: Should you use field injection or constructor injection in production Spring services?
questions.title: Field vs Constructor Injection Spring | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Prefer constructor injection over @Autowired field injection. Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit, enables immutable final fields, works cleanly with @InjectMocks in tests, and fails fast if a dependency is missing — at startup rather than at runtime.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know Spring best practices and can articulate the testability and immutability advantages of constructor injection
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Defending field injection because it requires less code — missing the testability, immutability, and compile-time safety benefits
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect constructor injection to test simplicity: @InjectMocks works cleanly, and manual test setup is trivial with explicit constructors

sections.title: Why Constructor Injection is the Spring Standard
sections.content:
**Constructor injection** is the recommended approach for Spring services because it makes dependencies **explicit and immutable**. When you declare dependencies as constructor parameters and assign them to final fields, you prevent accidental reassignment and make it clear what the class needs to function.

Spring's own documentation favors this pattern. **Field injection** with @Autowired looks concise but hides dependencies, allows mutable state, and can lead to circular dependency issues that only surface at runtime. From a testing perspective, constructor injection shines: you can create the service in tests by simply calling the constructor with mocks — no Spring context needed, no reflection magic. **@InjectMocks** aligns with this pattern, using constructor injection as its first strategy. In contrast, field injection requires reflection hacks in tests or forces you to load a Spring context with @MockBean, slowing tests significantly.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Constructor Injection|~The preferred style|final fields|immutable and testable|new in a plain test
blue|Field Injection|~Avoid in production|needs reflection|hidden dependencies|hard to instantiate
emerald|For Tests|~InjectMocks adapts|prefers constructor|falls back to field|matches by type

sections.title: Constructor Injection vs Field Injection
When to Choose Constructor Injection
sections.content:
Use **constructor injection** for all mandatory dependencies in production Spring services. If your service has **required collaborators** (repositories, gateways, validators), declare them as constructor parameters and final fields. This forces callers to provide them and prevents partially constructed objects.

Use **setter injection** only for truly optional dependencies — those that have sensible defaults and don't break core functionality if missing. In tests, constructor injection allows you to create the service with **plain Java constructors** — no annotations, no context loading. For integration tests where you need Spring wiring, constructor injection still works seamlessly with @MockBean.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Choosing Field Injection for Brevity**: Freshers pick @Autowired field injection because it's fewer lines of code, not realizing they're sacrificing testability and immutability.
- **Mixing Injection Types**: Using constructor injection for some dependencies and field injection for others creates inconsistency and confusion about which are mandatory.
- **Not Using Final Fields**: Declaring constructor-injected dependencies without final allows accidental reassignment and signals to readers that the field might change, when it shouldn't.
- **Ignoring Circular Dependencies**: Field injection can mask circular dependency issues until runtime; constructor injection surfaces them immediately during Spring context startup.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Explicit Dependencies**: Constructor parameters make it obvious what a class needs — no hidden coupling via @Autowired fields
- **Immutability**: Constructor injection enables final fields, preventing accidental reassignment and making the service thread-safe
- **Test Simplicity**: Unit tests can instantiate the service with plain constructors — no Spring context, no reflection
- **Fail Fast**: Missing dependencies cause startup failure with constructor injection; field injection fails at first use with NPE
- **@InjectMocks Alignment**: Mockito's @InjectMocks tries constructor injection first, so it works cleanly with constructor-based services
- **Spring 4.3+ Auto-Wiring**: Single-constructor classes don't need @Autowired annotation — Spring injects automatically
- **Circular Dependency Detection**: Constructor injection forces you to break circular dependencies; field injection hides them until runtime

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: In production Spring services, you should always prefer constructor injection over field injection. The main reason is that constructor injection makes your dependencies explicit and visible. When you declare dependencies as constructor parameters and assign them to final fields, anyone reading the code immediately sees what the service needs to work. Field injection with at-Autowired hides those dependencies inside the class, making it harder to understand the coupling. From a testing perspective, constructor injection is far simpler. In unit tests, you can just create the service by calling the constructor with your mocks — no need for Spring context, no reflection tricks. At-InjectMocks works cleanly because it tries constructor injection first. With field injection, you'd need to load the entire Spring context using at-MockBean or use reflection to set private fields, both of which slow down tests. Constructor injection also gives you immutability. You mark fields as final, which prevents accidental reassignment and makes the service thread-safe. Field injection forces you to use mutable fields. Finally, constructor injection fails fast. If a required dependency is missing, Spring throws an error during startup. With field injection, you get a NullPointerException at runtime when the code first tries to use the missing dependency. The Spring team recommends constructor injection in their official docs, and it's the pattern you'll see in well-maintained codebases.

questions.question: How do you manually inject mocks without using @InjectMocks?
questions.title: Manual Mock Injection Without @InjectMocks | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: Create the class under test manually in @BeforeEach, passing mocks as constructor arguments. This is explicit, debuggable, and fails loudly if arguments don't match. Preferred for complex setups where @InjectMocks silent failure would be hard to debug.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness that @InjectMocks is optional and that manual construction can be clearer for complex scenarios
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always using @InjectMocks without recognizing when explicit construction is simpler and safer
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Argue for explicit control when the test has conditional logic or multiple configurations of the same class

sections.title: Manual Mock Injection for Explicit Control
sections.content:
Manual mock injection means you create the test subject yourself in **@BeforeEach**, passing mocks directly as constructor arguments. You create mocks using **@Mock** annotations or **Mockito.mock()**, then instantiate your service with a plain constructor call. This approach gives you complete visibility into the wiring — no hidden Mockito resolution logic, no silent failures. If you pass the wrong type or forget a dependency, the **compiler catches it immediately**. Manual injection is especially valuable when you need **different configurations** of the same service across tests, or when the service has **conditional initialization logic** that @InjectMocks can't handle.

Think of it as choosing explicitness over convenience: a few extra lines of code in exchange for zero ambiguity and instant compile-time feedback.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Manual Wiring|~No annotation|new Service of mocks|an explicit constructor|full control
blue|Why Bother|~Clarity|obvious dependencies|no reflection magic|easy to debug
emerald|Trade-off|~More typing|update on signature change|InjectMocks is shorter|both are valid

sections.title: Manual Injection vs @InjectMocks
When Manual Injection is Better
sections.content:
Choose manual injection when your tests need **multiple configurations** of the same service — for example, testing behavior with and without an optional dependency.

Use it when the service has **complex constructors** with multiple overloads or factory methods that @InjectMocks can't resolve reliably.

Prefer manual injection in **parameterized tests** where you loop through different mock setups — creating the service inside the test method makes each iteration independent. Finally, use it when you're **new to Mockito** and want to understand exactly how your test objects are wired before relying on annotation magic.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Recreating Mocks in @BeforeEach**: Freshers sometimes call Mockito.mock() inside setUp() without using @Mock annotations, losing the automatic cleanup that MockitoExtension provides.
- **Forgetting @ExtendWith**: Even when manually constructing the service, you still need MockitoExtension to process @Mock annotations — without it, all mocks are null.
- **Over-Using Manual Injection**: Writing manual setup for every test when @InjectMocks would work fine — this adds boilerplate without benefit. Use manual injection when it actually solves a problem, not as a blanket rule.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Explicit Wiring**: You see exactly which mock is passed to which constructor parameter — no hidden resolution
- **Compile-Time Safety**: Type mismatches and missing arguments fail at compile time, not at runtime
- **Test Isolation**: Each test can create a different configuration of the service without affecting others
- **No Silent Failures**: If a mock isn't wired, you get a compiler error or immediate NPE, not a confusing failure later
- **@Mock Still Useful**: You still use @Mock to create mocks and @ExtendWith for cleanup — manual injection only affects the service construction
- **Parameterized Tests**: Manual construction in test methods allows easy variation of dependencies per test case
- **Debugging Simplicity**: When a test fails, you can step through the constructor call and see exactly what was passed

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To manually inject mocks without at-InjectMocks, you create the test subject yourself in the at-BeforeEach method by calling its constructor with the mocks as arguments. First, you declare your mocks using at-Mock annotations or Mockito.mock calls. Then, in setUp, you instantiate the service with a plain constructor call, passing the mocks explicitly. For example, if I'm testing OrderService, I'd create the paymentGateway and inventoryRepo mocks, then do orderService equals new OrderService with those mocks as parameters. This approach gives you complete control and makes the wiring obvious. If you pass the wrong type or forget a dependency, the compiler catches it immediately — you don't have to wait for a runtime NPE. Manual injection is especially useful when you need different configurations of the same service across tests. Maybe one test needs the service with an email sender, another without. With manual construction, you just create two different instances in the respective test methods. It's a few extra lines of code, but you get zero ambiguity and instant feedback. I still use at-Mock annotations for creating the mocks themselves because MockitoExtension handles cleanup automatically. Manual injection only replaces the at-InjectMocks step. This pattern is common in teams that value explicitness over annotation magic.

questions.question: What is @MockBean in Spring Boot testing and how does it differ from @Mock?
questions.title: @MockBean vs @Mock Spring Boot | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: @MockBean replaces a bean in the Spring application context with a Mockito mock. @Mock creates a standalone Mockito mock without loading Spring. Use @Mock for unit tests (fast), @MockBean for integration tests where the Spring context must be loaded.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the boundary between unit tests and Spring integration tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @MockBean in unit tests — unnecessarily loads the Spring context, making tests slow
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @MockBean invalidates the Spring context cache, causing re-load — a performance concern in large test suites

sections.title: Understanding @MockBean in Spring Boot Tests
sections.content:
**@MockBean** is a Spring Boot testing annotation that replaces a real bean in the **Spring application context** with a Mockito mock. When Spring starts for your test, it injects this mock wherever the real bean would normally be autowired. This is essential for **integration tests** where you need the Spring wiring and lifecycle but want to isolate external dependencies like databases or HTTP clients. In contrast, **@Mock** is a pure Mockito annotation that creates a mock without involving Spring at all — it's for **unit tests** where you manually construct the class under test.

The key difference: @MockBean forces Spring to load and configure the application context, which takes seconds. @Mock has zero Spring overhead — tests run in milliseconds. A hidden cost of @MockBean: it **invalidates the Spring context cache**. Each unique combination of @MockBean definitions creates a new context, slowing down test suites with dozens of test classes.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|the Mock annotation|~Plain Mockito|no Spring context|fast unit test|the ExtendWith extension
blue|the MockBean annotation|~Spring context|replaces a bean|integration or slice|slower startup
emerald|Pick Rule|~Default to Mock|MockBean needs context|use with SpringBootTest|or WebMvcTest

sections.title: @Mock vs @MockBean in Tests
When to Use @Mock vs @MockBean
sections.content:
Use **@Mock** for unit tests where you test a single class in isolation. If you're manually constructing the service with mocks as constructor arguments, @Mock is the right choice — tests run in milliseconds because there's no Spring overhead.

Use **@MockBean** for integration tests where you need Spring's dependency injection, transaction management, or web layer. For example, testing a **@RestController** with MockMvc requires the Spring context, and you'd use @MockBean to replace the service layer with a mock. Also use @MockBean when testing **@Transactional** behavior or Spring Data repository queries where you need the real JPA/JDBC wiring but want to mock external HTTP calls.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @MockBean in Plain Unit Tests**: Freshers add @MockBean to a test class that has no @SpringBootTest or slice annotation. The annotation does nothing, leaving the field null and causing NPE. @MockBean only works in Spring Boot test contexts.
- **Not Understanding the Performance Cost**: Using @MockBean in every test class because it feels familiar, not realizing each unique @MockBean configuration invalidates the context cache. A 50-test suite can end up loading the context 15 times, turning a 10-second suite into a 2-minute one.
- **Mixing @Mock and @MockBean Inconsistently**: Declaring some mocks with @Mock and others with @MockBean in the same test class without a clear reason, making it unclear which require Spring context and which don't.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@Mock is Mockito-Only**: Creates a standalone mock with no Spring involvement — for unit tests where you manually construct the class under test
- **@MockBean is Spring Boot-Specific**: Replaces a bean in the Spring application context with a mock — requires @SpringBootTest or a test slice annotation
- **Performance Impact**: @MockBean forces Spring context loading, adding 2-5 seconds per test class. @Mock tests run in milliseconds
- **Context Cache Invalidation**: Each unique @MockBean configuration creates a new context. Overusing @MockBean in large test suites causes severe slowdown
- **Integration Test Use Case**: @MockBean is ideal for testing controllers, transaction boundaries, or Spring Data repositories where Spring wiring is needed
- **@ExtendWith Requirement**: @Mock requires @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class). @MockBean requires @SpringBootTest or similar
- **Autowiring Behavior**: With @MockBean, other Spring beans autowired in the test receive the mock, not the real implementation

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The key difference between at-Mock and at-MockBean is whether you're loading the Spring application context. At-Mock is a pure Mockito annotation that creates a mock without involving Spring at all. You use it in unit tests where you manually construct the class you're testing, passing mocks as constructor arguments. These tests run in milliseconds because there's no Spring overhead. At-MockBean is a Spring Boot annotation that replaces a real bean in the application context with a Mockito mock. When you run the test, Spring starts up, loads all the beans, but substitutes the at-MockBean instances wherever they'd normally be autowired. You use at-MockBean in integration tests where you need Spring's dependency injection, like testing a RestController with MockMvc or verifying transactional behavior. The trade-off is speed. At-MockBean forces the context to load, which takes a few seconds per test class. There's also a hidden cost: at-MockBean invalidates the Spring context cache. If you have 20 test classes each with different at-MockBean configurations, Spring loads the context 20 times instead of reusing it, which can slow your test suite significantly. So the rule of thumb is: use at-Mock for fast unit tests where you're testing a single class, and at-MockBean for integration tests where you actually need Spring's wiring but want to mock external dependencies like databases or HTTP clients.

questions.question: What happens when @InjectMocks cannot inject a mock?
questions.title: @InjectMocks Silent Injection Failure
questions.direct_answer: Mockito silently skips the injection and leaves the field null, causing NullPointerException in tests. Using @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) with strict stubs helps surface these issues earlier by failing on unused mocks.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you are aware of this silent failure mode that causes confusing NullPointerExceptions in tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming @InjectMocks will throw a clear error if injection fails — it does not, it silently continues
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that strict stubbing mode helps indirectly by failing on unused stubs, and that constructor injection in production code avoids this entirely

sections.title: Silent Failure Mode of @InjectMocks
sections.content:
When **@InjectMocks** cannot inject a mock — because there's no matching constructor, no matching setter, and no matching field — it doesn't throw an exception. Instead, it **silently creates the test subject** and leaves the unmatched dependency fields as **null**. This is Mockito's design choice: it assumes you might be doing partial injection or have other setup logic.

The problem: you don't discover the failure until your test executes and tries to call a method on that null field, resulting in a **NullPointerException** with no clear indication that injection failed. This is especially confusing for freshers who expect annotation-driven tools to fail fast. The best defense is **constructor injection in production code** — Mockito's first injection phase, which fails at compile time if types don't match. The second defense is **strict stubbing** via MockitoExtension, which fails tests that have unused stubs or unnecessary stubbing, indirectly catching some injection failures earlier.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Silent Failure|~No error thrown|the field stays null|the test NPEs later|hard to debug
blue|Why It Happens|~No match found|a type mismatch|a name mismatch|a missing Mock field
emerald|The Fix|~Make it explicit|check the Mock is declared|prefer constructor|or wire manually

sections.title: Silent Injection Failure Example
How to Avoid Silent Injection Failures
sections.content:
Always use **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)** — it enables strict stubbing by default in modern Mockito, which fails tests on unused stubs. This indirectly catches some injection issues.

Prefer **constructor injection** in production code with all dependencies as constructor parameters, which aligns with Mockito's first injection phase and fails at compile time if you pass the wrong type. When you have **complex multi-constructor scenarios**, skip @InjectMocks entirely and use **manual construction** in @BeforeEach — explicitly call the constructor with mocks, making wiring visible and compile-time checked. Finally, if you see an NPE in a test on a field that should be mocked, **check field name spelling** — typos between @Mock field name and the class's field name cause silent injection failure.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Trusting @InjectMocks to Fail Loudly**: Freshers assume any issue with dependency wiring will throw an exception during test setup. It doesn't — you get an NPE during test execution instead.
- **Typos in Mock Field Names**: Declaring a mock with a typo like auditLoger when the class field is auditLogger. Mockito can't match by name, so it leaves the field null.
- **Not Using @ExtendWith**: Forgetting @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) means Mockito doesn't process annotations, so all @Mock and @InjectMocks fields are null. The error looks like an injection failure but is actually a setup failure.
- **Ignoring Constructor Injection**: Continuing to use field injection in production code because it's familiar, not realizing constructor injection would prevent all these silent test failures.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Silent Null Assignment**: If @InjectMocks can't inject a mock, it leaves the field null without throwing an error
- **Runtime NPE**: The failure surfaces as NullPointerException when the test tries to use the null dependency
- **Constructor Injection Defense**: Using constructor injection in production code makes Mockito's first phase succeed and fails at compile time if types mismatch
- **Strict Stubbing Helps**: MockitoExtension enables strict mode, which fails on unused stubs, indirectly catching some injection issues earlier
- **Manual Construction Alternative**: Skip @InjectMocks for complex scenarios and explicitly construct the service in @BeforeEach
- **Name Matching Pitfall**: Typos in @Mock field names prevent field injection, leaving dependencies null
- **@ExtendWith is Mandatory**: Without MockitoExtension, annotations aren't processed and all fields remain null

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When at-InjectMocks can't inject a mock, Mockito doesn't throw an error. It just creates the test subject and leaves the unmatched fields as null. You won't discover the problem until your test runs and tries to call a method on that null dependency, which throws a NullPointerException. This is really confusing for freshers because you expect annotation-driven tools to fail fast if something's wrong. The reason Mockito does this is it assumes you might be doing partial injection or have other setup logic, so it doesn't want to block you. The best way to avoid this is to use constructor injection in your production code. When all dependencies are constructor parameters, Mockito's first injection phase works cleanly. If you pass the wrong type or forget a dependency, the compiler catches it before you even run the test. Another defense is strict stubbing, which is enabled by default when you use at-ExtendWith with MockitoExtension. Strict mode fails tests that have unused stubs or unnecessary stubbing, which indirectly catches some injection problems earlier. If you have a complex scenario with multiple constructors or conditional logic, skip at-InjectMocks entirely and manually construct the service in at-BeforeEach. Just call the constructor explicitly with your mocks as arguments. That way, any wiring mistake is immediately visible, and you get compile-time validation. So the key takeaway is: don't assume at-InjectMocks will tell you if something's wrong. It fails silently and leaves you with a runtime NPE.

questions.question: How does Mockito decide between constructor injection and field injection for @InjectMocks?
questions.title: Constructor vs Field Injection in @InjectMocks
questions.direct_answer: Mockito tries constructor injection first (using the largest constructor that matches available mocks), then setter injection, then field injection as a fallback. Constructor injection is safest because it makes dependencies explicit and fails at compile time if types don't match.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Mockito's injection resolution order and why constructor injection is the safest option
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming Mockito always uses field injection; not knowing that constructor injection is attempted first and is safer
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect this to Spring's own injection preference: constructor injection is favored in both production Spring code and Mockito tests for the same reason — it makes dependencies explicit

sections.title: Mockito's Three-Phase Injection Strategy
sections.content:
When you use **@InjectMocks**, Mockito follows a priority order: **constructor injection**, then **setter injection**, then **field injection**. First, it scans the test subject class for constructors and picks the **largest constructor** that it can fully satisfy with available @Mock fields, matching by type. If it finds one, it calls that constructor and the job is done. If no constructor matches, Mockito looks for **setter methods** — methods named like setDependencyName() — and calls them with matching mocks. As a last resort, it uses **reflection to directly assign** mocks to fields, bypassing encapsulation. This order mirrors best practices: constructor injection is the safest because it forces **compile-time validation** and makes dependencies explicit. Setter injection is for optional dependencies. Field injection is a fallback that relies on reflection and has no compile-time checks.

The key insight: if you write production code with constructor injection, Mockito's first phase succeeds reliably, and you avoid the silent failures of the fallback phases.

sections.title: Injection Order in Action
Choosing the Right Injection Strategy
sections.content:
Use **constructor injection** for all mandatory dependencies in production code — it aligns with Mockito's first phase and makes dependencies explicit. Mockito picks the largest constructor it can satisfy, so if you have multiple constructors, the one with the most parameters matching @Mock types wins.

Use **setter injection** only for truly optional dependencies that have sensible defaults. Mockito calls matching setters after constructor injection completes.

Avoid relying on **field injection** in production code — while Mockito can handle it as a fallback, it bypasses encapsulation and offers no compile-time validation. If you find yourself needing precise control over which mocks go where, skip @InjectMocks and use manual construction in @BeforeEach.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming Field Injection is First**: Freshers think Mockito directly assigns mocks to fields because that's what Spring does with @Autowired field injection. Mockito actually tries constructors first.
- **Multiple Constructors Without Clarity**: Having several constructors without understanding that Mockito picks the largest one that matches available mocks, which can inject unintended configurations.
- **Mixing Injection Styles Randomly**: Using constructor injection for some dependencies and field injection for others without a clear pattern, making tests unpredictable.
- **Not Marking Optional Dependencies**: Declaring all dependencies as constructor parameters, even optional ones, forcing test setup to provide mocks for features not relevant to the test.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Constructor First**: Mockito tries constructor injection before any other strategy, picking the largest constructor that matches available mocks
- **Setter Second**: If no constructor matches, Mockito looks for setter methods named like setDependencyName() and calls them
- **Field Last**: Field injection via reflection is the fallback, used only if constructor and setter injection both fail
- **Type Matching Only**: Mockito matches by type, not by field name, so having two mocks of the same type causes ambiguity
- **Largest Constructor Wins**: If multiple constructors could be satisfied, Mockito picks the one with the most parameters
- **Aligns with Spring Best Practices**: Spring also favors constructor injection for the same reasons — explicitness and immutability
- **Manual Override**: For precise control, skip @InjectMocks and manually construct the service in @BeforeEach with explicit constructor calls

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Mockito decides between injection strategies using a three-phase order. First, it tries constructor injection. It scans your class for constructors and picks the largest one that it can fully satisfy with the available at-Mock fields, matching by type. If it finds a matching constructor, it calls that and you're done. If no constructor matches, Mockito moves to phase two: setter injection. It looks for methods named like setDependencyName and calls them with the appropriate mocks. If that also fails, it falls back to field injection, using reflection to directly assign mocks to fields, even private ones. The reason constructor injection is safest is that it makes dependencies explicit and gives you compile-time validation. If you pass the wrong type or forget a dependency, the compiler catches it immediately. Setter injection is for optional dependencies that have defaults. Field injection is a last resort that bypasses encapsulation and has no compile-time checks. This order mirrors Spring's own recommendations. Spring favors constructor injection for the exact same reasons — it forces you to declare what the class needs upfront. So if you write production code with constructor injection, Mockito's first phase succeeds cleanly, and you avoid the silent failures that happen when it has to fall back to field injection. For complex scenarios where you need precise control, I'd skip at-InjectMocks and just manually call the constructor in at-BeforeEach.

sections.title: Testing Constructor-Injected Classes Without @InjectMocks
sections.content:
When your production class uses **constructor injection**, testing it without @InjectMocks is straightforward and explicit. You create mocks using **@Mock annotations** (processed by MockitoExtension) or **Mockito.mock()** calls, then in your **@BeforeEach** method, you instantiate the test subject by calling its constructor directly with the mocks as arguments.

This approach is **self-documenting**: anyone reading the test sees exactly which mock goes to which constructor parameter. It's **compile-time safe**: if you pass the wrong type or forget an argument, the code won't compile. It eliminates the **silent failure risk** of @InjectMocks, where injection failures leave fields null and cause NPE at runtime. Many teams prefer this explicit style because it removes a layer of annotation magic and makes tests easier to debug when something goes wrong.

sections.title: Explicit Constructor Injection in Tests
When to Choose Explicit Over @InjectMocks
sections.content:
Use explicit constructor calls when you have **complex test scenarios** that need different configurations of the same service — just create multiple instances in individual test methods with different mock setups.

Prefer explicit construction when you're new to Mockito and want to **understand the wiring** before relying on annotations.

Use it when your class has **multiple constructors** and you want to test each one separately — @InjectMocks picks the largest matching constructor automatically, but explicit calls let you choose. Finally, use explicit construction in **parameterized tests** or **test factories** where you generate test subjects programmatically.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting @ExtendWith**: Even when manually constructing the service, you still need @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) to process @Mock annotations. Without it, all mocks are null.
- **Creating New Mocks in setUp**: Calling Mockito.mock() inside @BeforeEach without using @Mock annotations loses the automatic cleanup and reset that MockitoExtension provides between tests.
- **Over-Engineering Simple Tests**: Using explicit construction for every single test when @InjectMocks would work fine, adding unnecessary boilerplate. Use explicit construction when it solves a real problem, not as dogma.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Explicit Wiring**: Constructor call shows exactly which mock is passed to which parameter — zero ambiguity
- **Compile-Time Safety**: Type mismatches, wrong argument order, or missing arguments fail at compile time
- **No Silent Failures**: If a dependency isn't provided, the compiler catches it immediately, not at runtime with NPE
- **@Mock Still Useful**: Continue using @Mock annotations for creating mocks — MockitoExtension handles initialization and cleanup
- **Flexible Configuration**: Easy to create different service configurations per test by calling the constructor with different arguments
- **Debugging Simplicity**: When a test fails, you can step through the constructor call and see exactly what was passed
- **Team Preference**: Many teams prefer this explicit style for transparency and ease of onboarding new developers

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To test a class with constructor injection without using at-InjectMocks, you just create the test subject manually by calling its constructor. First, you declare your mocks using at-Mock annotations or Mockito.mock calls. Then, in the at-BeforeEach method, you instantiate the service by calling its constructor and passing the mocks as arguments. For example, if OrderService has a constructor that takes PaymentGateway and InventoryRepository, you'd write orderService equals new OrderService with paymentGateway and inventoryRepo as parameters. The advantage is that this wiring is completely explicit. Anyone reading the test can see exactly which mock goes where. If you pass the wrong type or forget an argument, the compiler catches it immediately — you don't have to wait for a runtime error. This approach eliminates the silent failure problem with at-InjectMocks, where injection fails but you only discover it when the test throws a NullPointerException. You still use at-Mock annotations to create the mocks because MockitoExtension handles initialization and cleanup automatically. The manual construction only replaces the at-InjectMocks step. I find this pattern especially useful when I need different configurations of the same service across tests. Instead of relying on at-InjectMocks to figure out the wiring, I just create the service with the exact mocks I need for each test. It's a few extra lines of code, but it makes the test self-documenting and much easier to debug.
